title: Tickets, timetables, transport
topic: buying a ticket, reading a timetable
why: This lesson opens the unit on travel at the train station: buying a one-way or round-trip ticket, reading a timetable with the 24-hour clock, and finding your way between the big Paris stations by métro. You'll also learn the numbers up to 1 000 for prices and distances, and use the passé composé to explain a missed train.

At the station: buying a ticket

France has a dense rail network: high-speed trains between the big cities, regional trains (le TER) for smaller towns. Whether you buy your ticket at the counter (le guichet), at a machine or on your phone, the words are the same.

FrenchEnglish
un billeta ticket
un aller simplea one-way ticket
un aller-retoura round-trip ticket
en première / en seconde (classe)in first / second class
une place côté fenêtrea window seat
une place côté couloiran aisle seat
la voiture 12, place 45car 12, seat 45
le train à grande vitessethe high-speed train
le TERthe regional train

Watch the false friend: on a train, la voiture is the carriage (\"car\" in American English, \"coach\" in British English). Your ticket says voiture 12: that's where you sit, not a car park!

Bonjour, je voudrais un aller-retour pour Lyon, s'il vous plaît.Hello, I'd like a round-trip ticket to Lyon, please.
— Vous voulez une place côté fenêtre ou côté couloir ? — Côté fenêtre, s'il vous plaît.—Would you like a window seat or an aisle seat? —A window seat, please.
C'est combien, un aller simple pour Bordeaux en seconde ?How much is a one-way ticket to Bordeaux in second class?

Use pour with the destination: un billet pour Lyon, le train pour Marseille. And keep je voudrais, your polite formula, for asking: je veux sounds too blunt at a counter.

", "

Reading the timetable

FrenchEnglish
le départ / l'arrivée (f.)departure / arrival
le quaithe platform
la voiethe track (voie 7 on the board)
la correspondancethe connection, the change
à l'heureon time
en retardlate, delayed
annulé / annuléecancelled
le contrôleur / la contrôleusethe ticket inspector, the conductor

Timetables always use the 24-hour clock, written with an h: 14 h 52 is read quatorze heures cinquante-deux. To ask about times, learn this question as it is (questions with the verb before the subject are studied in the next lesson):

À quelle heure part le prochain train pour Lyon ?What time does the next train to Lyon leave?
Le train de 14 h 52 a vingt minutes de retard.The 2:52 p.m. train is twenty minutes late.
Il y a une correspondance à Lyon : vous changez de train.There's a connection in Lyon: you change trains.

Numbers up to 1 000

For prices and distances, you need hundreds. Cent takes an -s when it's multiplied and ends the number (deux cents), but not when another number follows (deux cent cinquante). Mille never takes an -s, and you never say \"un mille\".

NumberIn words
100cent
101cent un
200deux cents
250deux cent cinquante
480quatre cent quatre-vingts
999neuf cent quatre-vingt-dix-neuf
1 000mille
1 200mille deux cents

French writes a space between thousands and a comma for decimals: 1 000 km, 148,50 €. The opposite of English (1,000 km, €148.50).

", "

In Paris: the big stations and the métro

Paris has several big train stations, each serving one part of the country. Their names tell you where the trains go, roughly:

StationTrains to…
la gare de LyonLyon, Marseille, Nice, the Alps
la gare du NordLille, the north, Belgium, London
la gare de l'EstStrasbourg, the east
la gare MontparnasseBordeaux, Rennes, Nantes, the west
la gare Saint-LazareNormandy

Note the contractions: la gare de Lyon, but la gare du Nord (de + le). To get from one station to another, take the métro. Each line has a number, and each direction is named after the last stop: la ligne 1, direction Château de Vincennes.

Pour aller à la gare de Lyon, vous prenez la ligne 4 jusqu'à Châtelet, puis vous changez à Châtelet et vous prenez la ligne 1, direction Château de Vincennes.To get to the Gare de Lyon, you take line 4 to Châtelet, then you change at Châtelet and take line 1 toward Château de Vincennes.

When you miss your train

The passé composé is perfect for travel trouble. Rater (informal) or manquer means to miss:

J'ai raté mon train ! Il est parti à 9 h 07 et je suis arrivé à 9 h 10.I missed my train! It left at 9:07 and I got there at 9:10.
Notre train était annulé, alors nous avons dû prendre le suivant.Our train was cancelled, so we had to take the next one.

Lyon is about 460 kilometers from Paris: quatre cent soixante kilomètres. By high-speed train, it takes about two hours.
